Transcript: Right. Linguistic relativity - the claim that the language you happen to speak shapes the thought you are able to have. And I want to begin by being clear about why anyone ever cared about it, because that turns out to matter for how we score the debate at the end. Nobody was ever excited by the weak reading, the one where language nudges your attention a little. What drew people in was the strong promise - that speakers of different languages inhabit genuinely different worlds, that certain thoughts are simply unavailable to you because your grammar has no room for them. Whorf put it roughly that way, and that formulation was, in the old phrase, a hostage to fortune.

The experiments came. And the first serious objection came from Pinker, who argued that the whole enterprise was circular - you probe a person's thought with a task whose instructions and whose response are themselves linguistic, so what you have measured is language twice over, not language and then thought. Now, I think that charge lands against the early colour-naming work. I do not think it touches what came afterwards.

What came afterwards is the interference paradigm. Take Russian, which obliges its speakers to distinguish two blues, a lighter and a darker, where English has one word. Russian speakers are reliably quicker at telling two shades apart when the pair straddles that category boundary. Not a naming effect - a discrimination effect, measured in milliseconds. But, and this is where the argument turns, give them a string of digits to hold in memory while they do it, and the advantage disappears. Load the verbal channel and the effect switches off.

So what is left standing? Not Whorf. What is left is smaller and, I would say, far more interesting - habitual language is recruited, quietly, as a working resource while a task is under way. Meddling, not moulding. Relativity as a claim about processing rather than about competence; about which discriminations come cheaply, never about which ones are possible.

And there are colleagues who take that same result the other way, who say that an effect you can abolish with a memory load was never about thought at all, only about labels lying ready to hand. I understand the reasoning. I don't go along with it - an effect that operates in every unloaded moment of ordinary life is not made trivial by the fact that you can jam it in a laboratory.

But notice the bill. The version left standing cannot do the job the hypothesis was originally hired for. It will not tell you that a Hopi speaker lives in a different universe, and it will not underwrite a single claim about untranslatable worldviews. It has bought its survival by surrendering exactly the territory that made it famous.
prompt: [Academic Talk — Psycholinguistics] Which version of linguistic relativity does the lecturer regard as surviving the evidence he describes?
choices: The claim that the categories a speaker's language supplies fix which perceptual discriminations that speaker is capable of making at all.
The claim that the Russian advantage at the blue boundary is a matter of how the shades are named rather than of how they are seen.
The claim that habitual language is drawn on as a working resource while a task is in progress, making some discriminations cheaper without making any of them impossible.
The claim that verbal interference erases the Russian advantage because the two colour categories were never learned deeply enough to become automatic.
correct_answer: The claim that habitual language is drawn on as a working resource while a task is in progress, making some discriminations cheaper without making any of them impossible.
explanation: C2 rather than C1 because the answer is only available to a listener who tracks the argument through all three of its stages - the strong position stated in the opening, its complication by the interference result in the middle, and the deliberately narrowed form ('processing rather than competence') the lecturer then rescues - and who recognises that the surviving version is neither the original claim nor its outright denial; a listener who fixes on any single stage is offered a fluent wrong answer at every one of them.

choices: That an effect which a memory load can switch off is telling us about the ready availability of labels rather than about thought.
That Whorfian work is circular, because thought is being probed by means of a task that is itself linguistic.
That the interference findings show the early colour-naming studies to have been circular after all.
That the Russian speakers' advantage shows up only where the two shades fall on opposite sides of a category boundary.

prompt: [Academic Talk — Psycholinguistics] The lecturer says that Whorf's formulation was 'a hostage to fortune.' What does he mean by this?
choices: That the theory's fate was left to luck, since no experiment available at the time could have tested it either way.
That the claim had been seized on by admirers who cared more about its fame than about defending it accurately.
That Whorf held back the strongest form of his claim in order to shield it from the objections he expected.
That Whorf had committed himself so specifically that later evidence could be brought against him, as in the event it was.
correct_answer: That Whorf had committed himself so specifically that later evidence could be brought against him, as in the event it was.
explanation: C2 rather than C1 because the phrase is non-compositional and its everyday parts point elsewhere - 'fortune' reads as luck and 'hostage' as something seized, and both wrong readings are supplied as fluent options - so the phrase can only be settled by carrying it forward across a paragraph break to the section where the experiments do in fact come and collect on the commitment.
